submission.natural_language_explanation: L4/N147+ fires on relational vocabulary that places one thing against a reference: comparison/identity words (different, similar, other, various, separate, same), extent-or-degree words on the 'more' side of a scale (large, big, great, wide, long, greater, larger, longer, more, most, much, many, all, additional, increase), position/order words in time or space (further, later, next, following, continue, beyond, behind, throughout, close, top, end, rest, then, still), and the relational predicates that link a cause, a part or a result to its relatum (lead/leads/led/leading, part of, followed by, as a result, related, consistent). It stays near zero on intrinsic physical properties (red, blue, wooden, cold, old, nice, simple), on the decreasing side of a scale (small, short, narrow, low, few, less, least) and on nominalisations of the same notions (difference, similarity, variety, size, degree, leader).

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Section 3: tidepool survey routine. Reach the cove about an hour before low water, wearing boots with firm grip, and carry a slate, a pencil, and a bucket for shells that need a closer look. Walk the upper ledge first and count crabs in every pool you pass, writing each number on a waterproof card with the pool code. Take care on wet stone, keep your balance near surge channels, and call out shark sightings to the crew chief at once. Photograph each pool from the north side so shadows fall the same way in each picture, and rinse the lens if spray fogs the glass. Work downhill toward the surf as the water drops, moving slowly so limpets stay fixed to the rock and anemones keep their tentacles open. Record water temperature with the probe on a cord, dipping it elbow-deep and waiting ten heartbeats before reading the dial. Note gull flocks overhead, otter tracks in wet sand, and kelp beds torn loose by night storms. Eat lunch on dry rock above the foam line, drink from sealed bottles, and pack shells, weed, and rubbish back into sacks. After lunch, sketch the layout of each pool in pencil, marking boulders, channels, and weed clumps, and label each drawing with date, tide height, and your initials. Measure pool depth with a knotted rope, dropping it straight down and pinching the knot at the waterline, then lay the rope on sand to read the marks. List sea stars by color, count urchins in crevices, and note barnacle bands with chalk ticks on slate edges. If fog rolls in, sound the horn twice, gather the crew, and wait on high rock until the horn answers from shore. The following week, lay the cards on a bench in separate piles for each cove, and tally counts under lamplight with a friend checking each sum, where large pools at the south point held many more crabs than shallow pans near the stairs, a pattern the crew confirmed later in the season when revisiting the same transects after a storm. File the totals in the harbor office binder, sweep the floor, wash the buckets, and at the end of the day hang wetsuits on pegs and store the rest of the gear in lockers.
